newsitem.title: CHINA: China remarks on Hong Kong freedoms risky - Thatcher.
newsitem.headline: China remarks on Hong Kong freedoms risky - Thatcher.

text.p: China's statements implying that free speech in Hong Kong will be curbed after 1997 risked undermining the colony's foundations, former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher said on Thursday.
The success of the transfer of power in the British colony next year was in China's hands, she told a business conference in Beijing.
"Statements which imply that free speech will be qualified after 1997 risk undermining the foundations on which Hong Kong's enterprise society is built," she said.
"China will need to show great understanding for Hong Kong's traditions -- above all its tradition of free speech," she said.
Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule on July 1, 1997.

Thatcher did not refer to any specific comments by Beijing but China's Foreign Minister Qian Qichen raised an outcry in the British colony last month when he suggested Hong Kong would no longer be able to mark the anniversary of Beijing's June 4, 1989 crackdown on student-led protests for democracy.
Chinese officials later tried to backtrack from the remarks, made in an interview with the Asian Wall Street Journal.
Thatcher led the British government during the often bitter negotiations which eventually led to the 1984 agreement on the return of Hong Kong to China.
Under the accord, Beijing agreed to grant Hong Kong a "high degree" of autonomy for 50 years.
"The success of the transition is now in China's hands and in China's hands alone," Thatcher said.
She said China would be watched closely for any signs of failing to live up to its part of the agreement, though she added she was confident that would not be the case.
She also brushed aside Beijing criticism that such monitoring of its actions in Hong Kong was foreign interference in the territory.

"It's not a case of foreign governments' interfering in Hong Kong," she said. "It's a simple fact of life in the modern world...that events are subject to the most detailed scrutiny by television and a free press."
The former prime minister added that she was planning to be in Hong Kong to observe the transfer of power first hand.
